analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for investors to sue companies and their advisers over securities fraud.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for private securities fraud lawsuits. A defendant could only be forced to pay another defendant's share of damages if found to have knowingly committed fraud, and reckless conduct would no longer support full recovery. Investors would have to prove fraud intent by clear and convincing evidence, plead specific facts suggesting intent, and risk paying the other side's legal fees if they lost. It would also have barred class-action lawyers with conflicts of interest or paid referral arrangements and stopped class representatives from taking special shares of settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, their officers and directors, accounting firms, and investment banks. They would face fewer fraud lawsuits, and no single defendant could be forced to cover the full judgment unless proven to have knowingly defrauded investors. Losing defendants could collect their legal fees from plaintiffs who lose.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public companies, auditors, and investment banks

how_it_helps.text: Limits joint and several liability so a defendant pays only its own share of damages unless the court specifically finds it engaged in knowing securities fraud, defined to exclude reckless conduct.

Requires investors to prove fraudulent intent by clear and convincing evidence and to plead specific facts suggesting intent, and narrowly limits liability for people and firms who helped someone else's fraud.
Requires courts to award attorney fees and expenses to the prevailing party in most cases, so plaintiffs who lose can be made to pay the company's legal bills.
The bill's stated findings argue that excessive securities litigation burdens the economy, forces companies into bankruptcy, and discourages bankers and accountants from working with startup firms.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who were misled. Someone defrauded by a company whose executives were careless but not proven to have acted knowingly could recover far less or nothing, and the risk of paying the defendant's fees would deter many from suing at all.

drawbacks.text: Loser-pays fee shifting would expose defrauded investors to paying a corporation's legal bills if their case falls short, which would discourage many valid claims from ever being filed.

Requiring clear and convincing proof of intent and excluding reckless conduct would leave investors without recovery in cases involving serious mismanagement that falls short of deliberate fraud — including cases where the specific wrongdoer cannot be identified or is judgment-proof.

The bill does target some real abuses: class representatives would no longer get outsized shares of settlements, and lawyers with stock in the company being sued or who paid for client referrals would be barred. An honest supporter would acknowledge, though, that these narrower fixes are bundled with the much larger liability and fee changes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The class-representation and conflict-of-interest provisions address genuine problems in securities class actions. But the core of the bill — eliminating joint liability absent proof of knowing fraud, a higher evidentiary standard, and loser-pays fees — would shift the cost of corporate fraud from the companies and advisers responsible to the shareholders who lost money. Even the bill's own findings frame the goal as fewer lawsuits rather than better ones, so the likely trade is fewer abusive suits at the price of fewer valid ones.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees and then a subcommittee, where it sat; it never reached a committee vote or the House floor and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin introduced the bill on January 25, 1995, joined by Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Hall of Texas, Towns, Rush, and Brown of Ohio.
The House referred it to both the Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On February 21, 1995, the Commerce Committee sent the bill to its Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and no further action was recorded.
The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Under this bill, investors and the class-action lawyers who represent them came out ahead, because its liability and fee provisions never became law. In practical terms, though, the industry got much of what it wanted anyway: Congress passed very similar securities litigation reform later in 1995, which became law over a presidential veto — a well-known development outside the sources provided for this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors, though similar reforms passed anyway

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and its original cosponsors were Democrats, including four named in the introduced text, so sponsorship crossed party lines; there is no record of organized opposition because it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and their executives
industries.note: The bill would shield companies and their officers from joint liability and most securities fraud suits, with the savings coming directly out of the recovery available to investors who were misled. Its own findings describe the goal as reducing litigation against companies.

These professional advisers face securities suits for helping companies commit fraud; the bill would require proof they acted knowingly and deliberately for their own financial benefit, sharply limiting their exposure. Their reduced liability means investors bear more of the cost of fraud they helped conceal.

Loser-pays fee shifting, bans on lawyers with stock in the defendant or paid referrals, and limits on settlements would cut both the volume of cases and the fees available to firms that sue companies on behalf of shareholders. Their interest runs alongside ordinary investors' ability to recover losses.
